notes:
I've written notes for verses 28–29, 31, 34–38 and 43–54. Nothing I read covered verses 30, 32–33 or 39–42 in any useful way, so I've left those out, along with anything from Catholic, Orthodox, modern-scholarship or popular-teaching sources. My searches and page fetches ran out first.

Two things to know about the sources:
- The Enduring Word (David Guzik) page cut off before verse 28, so the Guzik points below come from search excerpts only.
- John Piper's sermon on verses 43–54 is summarised from the full page, so those points have the URL but no excerpt markers.

# John 4:28–54: Research notes

## 1. The traditional reading

**v. 28:**
- **Guzik:** The woman left her waterpot because she was so moved and so sure she would come back. He also says a detail like a forgotten waterpot is the kind of thing an eyewitness (John) would remember. Perhaps sensing the silent awkwardness of the disciples, the woman left her conversation with Jesus and went back into the city of Sychar. She left so impressed by her time with Jesus (and so certain she would return to him) that she left her waterpot at the well. The left-behind waterpot is the kind of small point remembered by an eyewitness. As one of the disciples to see this, John remembered this event clearly. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-4/)
- **Matthew Henry:** People who spread Christ's name shouldn't be held back by anything. He also reads her leaving the jar as caring little for worldly things. Those whose business it is to publish the name of Christ must not encumber or entangle themselves with any thing that will retard or hinder them therein. Those who are brought to the knowledge of Christ will show it by a holy contempt of this world and the things of it. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jhn/Jhn_004.cfm)
- **Henry, a second suggestion:** She left it in kindness to Christ, that he might have water to drink (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/4-35.html)
- **Barclay:** Leaving the jar showed two things: she was in a hurry to tell others, and she fully meant to come back. The fact that she left her water-pot showed two things. It showed that she was in a hurry to share this extraordinary experience, and it showed that she never dreamed of doing anything else but come back. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/john-4.html)
- **Jamieson, Fausset & Brown (quoted in the Light of Israel commentary):** She had earlier teased Jesus for having no water jar, and now she abandoned her own. Before, she had chided Jesus for not having one and now she forsook hers. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/4-30.html)
- **B. W. Johnson:** She had tasted the "living water" and forgot her need for well water. She had got a taste of the "living water," and forgot her need of the water of the well. (https://www.ccel.org/j/johnson_bw/ntc3/NTC304.HTM)

**v. 29:**
- **Piper:** She seems to tell everyone, even though she had been reluctant to talk about her past with Jesus. She also wonders aloud whether he might be the Messiah. it appears to be indiscriminate telling of everyone, in spite of how hesitant she was to talk to Jesus about her sordid life. She says he knew everything about her and wonders out loud if he might be the Messiah, the Christ. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-food-of-christ-is-to-give-eternal-life)

**v. 31:**
- **Henry:** Jesus put his work ahead of food. The chance to save souls made him forget how tired and hungry he was. this opportunity of saving souls made him forget his weariness and hunger. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jhn/Jhn_004.cfm)

**v. 34:**
- **Piper:** He ties "food" to "eternal life" in verse 36: Jesus's food is reaping eternal life. gathering fruit for eternal life [there's the link!], so that sower and reaper may rejoice together." Jesus is reaping eternal life. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-food-of-christ-is-to-give-eternal-life)

**v. 35:**
- **Guzik:** "Harvest" means many people were ready to enter God's kingdom, and the disciples should see themselves as reapers. "White" suggests grain that is fully ripe or even overripe. The idea of harvest meant that there were many people ready to be received into the Kingdom of God, and that the disciples should see themselves as workers – reapers – in that harvest. If they had the eyes to see it, the harvest was ready now – even white for harvest, implying that the grain was fully ripe or over ripe. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-4/)
- **Gill:** Jesus isn't talking about real crops here. He means a harvest of souls: the many Samaritans then coming across the fields. Christ here speaks not literally; for the fields could not be white at such a distance from harvest; but spiritually, of a harvest of souls (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/4-35.html)
- **Gill on "four months":** He takes it as a timing note: about eight months had passed since the last Passover, with four still to go. Our Lord had been in Jerusalem and Judea, about eight months from the last passover, and there remained four more to the next passover (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/4-35.htm)
- **Ellicott:** He agrees it is probably a time marker, not a proverb. He sees the Samaritans as the firstfruits of a bigger harvest. The Samaritans coming to Him are as the firstfruits, the earnest of the abundant sheaves which shall follow. Four months.—This gives us probably a note on time. There is no evidence that it was a proverbial saying (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/4-35.htm)
- **Coffman, Barclay and Chuck Smith:** All three picture the white-robed townspeople crossing the green fields as the "white" harvest. The white-clad multitude passing over the green fields between the village and the well had indeed turned them white (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/4-35.html)
- **Pulpit Commentary (as I read it):** The fields are "dead ripe" and will be lost unless they are reaped. "These fields will be sacrificed, these fruits will be wasted, these souls will be lost, unless they are reaped and brought into the heavenly garner." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/4-35.htm)

**vv. 36–37:**
- **Cambridge Bible:** It notes a textual question: some of the best manuscripts put "already" at the start of verse 36 ("already he that reapeth…"). 'Already' is the last word in the Greek sentence; and from very ancient times there has been a doubt whether it belongs to this sentence or the next. Some of the best MSS. give 'already' to the next sentence (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/4-35.htm)
- **Chuck Smith:** He links "one sows, another reaps" to Paul's teaching that one plants, another waters, and God gives the growth. Paul said, "One plants, one waters. God gives the increase." (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/4-35.html)

**v. 38:**
- **Pulpit Commentary (as I read it):** Before Samaria, Jesus had spent about eight months in Judea with no obvious results. The faith there was shallow and based on signs, and he didn't entrust himself to it. This makes our Lord to have spent some eight months since the Passover, either in Jerusalem or in the Judaean land, on his earliest mission, which as yet had brought no obvious results. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/4-35.htm)

**v. 44:**
- **Piper:** He takes "hometown" to mean Galilee. Because verse 44 begins with "for," he reads it as John's reason for the trip: Jesus deliberately went where he would be honoured less than in Samaria. Compare John 1:11, "He came to his own…" (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/go-your-son-will-live)

**v. 45:**
- **Piper:** The Galileans' "welcome" wasn't real honour. It was interest in his miracles, like the shallow "belief" in John 2:23–25 and his brothers in John 7:5. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/go-your-son-will-live)
- **Steven Cole (bible.org):** Someone can receive Jesus without truly believing in him. It's possible to receive Jesus without truly believing in Him. (https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-25-foxhole-faith-saving-faith-john-443-54)

**v. 46:**
- **"Royal official":** In Greek this is *basilikos*, from the word for "king." The Greek word for this official is basilikos, derived from basileus, which means "king." (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/4-48.html)
- **Utley:** He served the Herod family. This was a governmental official in the service of the Herod family. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/john-4.html)
- **Cole:** We don't know whether he was a Jew or a Gentile. Cole wonders whether he could be Manaen (Acts 13:1). We don't know whether he was a Jew or a Gentile, but he probably had some post in Herod's court. He could have been Manaen (https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-25-foxhole-faith-saving-faith-john-443-54)
- **Coffman:** He thinks the official was a Jew, because Jesus's "you" in verse 48 lumps him in with the Jews. suggesting that the nobleman himself was a Jew. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/4-48.html)

**v. 47:**
- **Trapp (as I read it):** He contrasts this man with the centurion of Matthew 8:8. This man insisted that Jesus come down, as if he must teach Christ how to work. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/4-48.html)
- **Deffinbaugh (bible.org):** He sets the two stories side by side. The centurion asked Jesus *not* to come; the official asked him to come. The Centurion urges Jesus not to come, but only to speak the word; the Royal Official urges Jesus to come. (https://bible.org/seriespage/11-jesus-heals-royal-official-s-son-john-443-54)

**v. 48:**
- **"You" is plural:** Jesus is speaking to Galileans in general, not just the official. The NET Bible, along with some other translations, indicates that the "you" in verse 48 is plural, and not singular. Jesus is therefore speaking to a larger audience than just the royal official. (https://bible.org/seriespage/11-jesus-heals-royal-official-s-son-john-443-54)
- **Barnes:** He contrasts the Galileans with the Samaritans. The Samaritans had believed without any miracle. (https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nrs/john/4-48.html)
- **Constable:** This is the only place John's Gospel uses "wonders." This is the only place in John's Gospel where "wonders" occurs. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/4-48.html)
- **Coffman:** "Signs" and "wonders" aren't two kinds of miracle. They are two sides of every miracle. Signs and wonders … is not a reference to two kinds of miracles, but rather to the two qualities in every miracle. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/4-48.html)
- **Utley:** The Greek has a strong double negative ("you will never believe"). This is a third class conditional sentence with a strong double negative. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/john-4.html)
- **Henry:** He calls it a "gentle rebuke," and notes the man didn't take offence or give up. as he did not take the reproof for an affront, so he did not take it for a denial, but still prosecuted his request (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/4-48.html)
- **Deffinbaugh:** He suggests Jesus spoke this way to break up a curious crowd and avoid stirring up messianic excitement too early. Our Lord's response to the official, as well as to those gathered, achieves His desire to disperse the crowd. (https://bible.org/seriespage/11-jesus-heals-royal-official-s-son-john-443-54)

**v. 49:**
- **Piper:** The man doesn't answer the rebuke. He just asks again. Piper compares Jesus testing the Syrophoenician woman (Mark 7:27). (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/go-your-son-will-live)
- **Deffinbaugh:** The official seemed to think Jesus could heal the boy only if he was there in person, not from about 20 miles away. The royal official seems to believe that Jesus can heal his son if He is at his side, but not from 20 miles away. (https://bible.org/seriespage/11-jesus-heals-royal-official-s-son-john-443-54)

**v. 50:**
- **Henry:** Now he sees no sign or wonder, and yet believes the wonder done. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/4-48.html)
- **Piper:** The man obeyed without asking anything more. Piper thinks something woke up in him when Jesus spoke with such authority. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/go-your-son-will-live)
- **Bridgeway:** Jesus accepted what little faith the man had (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/4-48.html)

**vv. 51–53:**
- **Piper:** Hearing the hour confirmed the man's faith, and his household came to believe as well. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/go-your-son-will-live)
- **Deffinbaugh:** This royal official came to the point where he was willing to take Jesus at His word, and he and his household became believers. (https://bible.org/seriespage/11-jesus-heals-royal-official-s-son-john-443-54)
- **Bible Hub "Questions" article:** It describes the man moving from sign-seeking to faith resting on Jesus's word. The royal official, however, transitions from sign-seeker to Word-based believer (https://biblehub.com/q/Why_did_Jesus_mention_signs_in_John_4_48.htm)

**v. 54:**
- **Henry:** This connects back to John 2:11. Each sign came soon after Jesus returned from Judea. that was soon after his first return out of Judea, this soon after his second. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/4-48.html)

## 2. Where Protestant teachers differ

I didn't find any sharp split along denominational lines. These are the real differences in emphasis I came across:

**v. 35: what the "white fields" stand for.**
- Most teachers say they are people ready to receive the gospel. Guzik says this (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-4/), and so does Henry (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jhn/Jhn_004.cfm).
- Constable (a dispensationalist evangelical) instead says they are people ripe for judgment. The whitened fields represent humankind in its condition of being ripe for divine judgment. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/4-35.html)

**v. 48: how strong was the official's faith?**
- **Adam Clarke (Methodist):** The man had some faith, just not enough. Our Lord does not tell this man that he had no faith, but that he had not enough. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/4-48.html)
- **Piper (Reformed Baptist):** The rebuke is aimed at a sign-seeking faith that isn't really faith. He doesn't commend the official at first. Jesus does not commend the man or the people around him. He is provoked at the sign-seeking false faith that abounds in Galilee. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/go-your-son-will-live)

**v. 48: what to make of seeking "signs and wonders" today.**
- **Spurgeon (Baptist):** He applies the verse against relying on dreams, voices or visions, and points people to Scripture instead. No, we must have done with this desire to see signs and wonders. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/4-48.html)
- **Guzik (Calvary Chapel, a charismatic-leaning evangelical church), on verse 35:** He quotes a different Spurgeon line that urges people to expect blessing now. "Expect a present blessing; believe that you will have it; go to work to get it, and do not be satisfied unless you do have it." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-4/)

## 3. Other views
Not found: I found nothing on netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, the Catholic or Orthodox sites, or about prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this passage.
